newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hani widow gets killers' amnesty hearing postponed.
newsitem.headline: Hani widow gets killers' amnesty hearing postponed.

text.p: An amnesty hearing for the killers of popular black anti-apartheid leader Chris Hani was postponed on Monday at his widow's request until August 11.

White right-wingers Clive Derby-Lewis and Janusz Walus are serving life terms for Hani's assassination on April 10, 1993. They were initially sentenced to death but this was commuted to life imprisonment.

Their amnesty appeal was due to be heard by Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission this week, but lawyers for Hani's widow Limpho said she had prior commitments in the United States and they needed more time to review documents before the amnesty panel.
Lawyers for Derby-Lewis and Polish immigrant Walus, who did not testify during their trial, are basing their request for amnesty on the grounds that the crime was politically motivated.

A senior lawyer for Hani's widow, George Bizos, told the commission he would oppose the amnesty application because he had documents to prove that Derby-Lewis and Walus "did not act on behalf or orders of any known political organisation".

Bizos added that at their trial the two had not revealed who had been behind the killing. He also said he had statements from right-wing and conservative leaders who had denied any role in the murder.
Hani, leader of the South African Communist Party until his death, was the most popular communist in the now-ruling African National Congress (ANC).
In 1991, he led the field in the ANC's internal election of an 82-member policy-making National Executive Committee, winning support from 95 per cent of delegates.
He also came second only to Deputy President Thabo Mbeki in the election to the ANC's 26-member shadow cabinet, known as the National Working Group.

About 500 supporters of the Communist Party chanted and danced in the Benoni City Hall east of Johannesburg where the hearing was held, while a handful of conservative whites sat quietly, some women knitting and surrounded by picnic hampers with sandwiches and flasks of coffee.

When Walus and Derby-Lewis entered the hall, the screams and jeers of the Communist supporters reached fever pitch and Hani's weeping 16-year-old daughter Nomakhwezi was ushered out of the hall by President Nelson Mandela's former wife, Winnie.

The truth commission was set up in 1995 to heal the wounds of South Africa's apartheid past by investigating human rights abuses on both sides of the racial divide. It has the power to grant amnesty to offenders who make full confessions.
